section: The example: World of Warcraft Avatar History
text:
The example: World of Warcraft Avatar History

Dataset: WoWAH — ~11M timestamped “heartbeats” (one snapshot every ~10 min, 2006–2009, 91k avatars)
Task: predict whether a player churns (no activity for two months) in month M+1
Unit of analysis: the (character, month) pair, built as a cross-product grid
Features: sessionization (SessionEncoder), monthly aggregates, zone-rarity / Gini location features, lag & diff features
Model: HistGradientBoostingClassifier + TableVectorizer, month-by-month temporal CV







Important


Model optimization is intentionally not the focus of this talk.

title: Skrub Data Ops: an application to player churn
section: Pain point 1 — Leakage in temporal feature engineering
text:
Pain point 1 — Leakage in temporal feature engineering

Features must only use data available at scoring time
Session detection and aggregations are stateful w.r.t. time: doing them once on the full table leaks the future
sklearn Pipeline cannot do this: X/y must exist before the pipeline starts, and wrangling lives outside
skrub docs warn explicitly: aggregation can introduce data leakage → wrap it in the DataOps plan
In the example: X and y are cut inside the plan (mark_as_X / mark_as_y), so each CV fold re-runs the feature code on training data only


This is the central difficulty of the example (main.py:90-186). If the target month is April, features may only be built from February data and earlier (main.py:136-143). The skrub sessionization doc (modules/multi_column_operations/sessionization.rst) carries a warning box saying aggregation leaks unless it is re-fit per fold — either wrapped in an sklearn transformer or done “with the skrub Data Ops framework”. DataOps bind the whole wrangling DAG to the prediction, so skb.cross_validate() re-executes the leakage-safe steps inside every fold automatically, instead of the user hand-rolling fold-by-fold feature construction.

Pain point 4 — One pipeline object, many inputs



Multi-input pipelines are usually scattered across scripts
Input methods can differ between model setup and production (read from file, fetch an API…)
The final DataOp behaves like one sklearn estimator: .fit(), save, load, skb.eval(env), skb.cross_validate(env)
Production: replay the exact trained DAG on new data, no need for glue code

  return pd.read_csv("path/to/file.csv")

def prod_loader():

loader = skrub.var("loader", draft_loader, becomes_default=True)
# build the DAG

Pain point 5 — Debugging a complex DAG

Data Ops work lazily: they need to evaluate all nodes in the DAG to run
Eager previews: pass a value to var() and every node shows its result immediately
skb.report() emits an HTML report: every node’s name, description, predecessors, fitted estimator, and data preview
On failure, the report shows the offending node and the traceback

section: Pain point 7 — Stay in your dataframe API inside the plan
text:
Pain point 7 — Stay in your dataframe API inside the plan

Frameworks usually force you to leave Polars once you enter “pipeline land”
DataOps are transparent: Polars methods are called directly on DataOps (historical_data.with_columns(...), .collect(), indexing, joins)
Python control flow (for month in ...) must be put in @deferred / apply_func functions
Deferred functions appear as one graph node — good for reports and caching

title: Predicting player churn in an MMORPG (WoW)
text:
In this blog post we will see how we can predict player churn in World of Warcraft (WoW), a subscription-based MMORPG that was released in 2004. More precisely, we are interested in predicting a player’s behavior in a given month, and decide whether there is a risk that they will stop playing the next month. To do so, we want to train a machine learning model that, given features based on each player and on the overall playerbase, will be able to predict whether player X will stop playing in a given month.
Through the post we will build a full machine learning pipeline: we use
polars for dataframe operations; skrub is used for data exploration, feature engineering and constructing the overall execution plan; scikit-learn is imported for the actual ML model; hyperparameter optimization is done using Optuna through skrub’s Data Ops.
To keep the focus of this post on the process rather than the code, most of the lower-level functions will be hidden in collapsible blocks. This includes much of the pre-processing and feature engineering, although important sections will be highlighted as needed. Additionally, some detail on the implementation will be omitted from this writeup; for detailed comments and rationale on the code refer to the repository.

title: Predicting player churn in an MMORPG (WoW)
section: 1 Modeling player churn
text:
1 Modeling player churn
Modeling user churn is a common application of machine learning models, though the definition of churn is typically business’ specific. In general, by “user churn” one refers to “a user that does not come back to the service”. In the context of this example, churn refers to those characters that are not found online after a certain amount of time, and that suspended their subscription.
As we do not have access to the actual subscription data, we assume that a player has suspended their subscription when they stop playing for two consecutive months. A single missing month is more likely a break than a cancellation, so a character that skips a month and then comes back is not considered churned.
For this post, we aggregate player behaviors at a monthly basis, and add a has_played flag that tells us if a player has played at least once during each month. From it, we derive two columns:

churn: the character has churned as of this month, i.e., has_played is False both in this month and in the previous one.
churn_next: the value of churn in the following month. This is the target that we want to predict.







Important



Our objective
Given a month (e.g., June), we want to use all the data up to the last day of the previous month (all months until May included) to predict whether a user will have churned as of July (i.e., their has_played flag will be False both in June and in July).



The idea is that, by knowing that user X is likely to churn, we should be able to use the month of June to apply some incentive to the user so they won’t churn. Note that, in the diagram, a character that is absent in the target month has only churned if it was also absent in the “gap month”.






WarningWhy the target is shifted



It is tempting to use churn itself as the target of the June row. However, the features of the June row are built from May, and churn for June is only true if the character was absent in May: any character with activity in May would be labeled “not churned” by construction, and the model would learn that from the missing values alone. Cross-validation scores looked excellent (ROC AUC around 0.95) for the wrong reason. Shifting the target one month forward removes the shortcut.


One caveat with this modeling strategy is that we are working with historical data, so we cannot actually apply said incentive and observe whether it has an impact like in a typical A/B test.

1.1 Building the churn dataset
We begin by adding two columns to the historical dataset: in the first we store each timestamp, truncated to have a monthly resolution; in the second we track the first month for each character. Additionally, we add a constant has_played column that acts as our “player was seen” flag.
We are interested in monthly snapshots, so the dataset is then reduced to select only the unique (character, month) pairs.






NoneData preparation (click to expand)







def make_data(df, interval="1mo"):
    """
    Prepare a dataframe that contains the months in which each player has
    actually played. The column "has_played" is then set to True for those months.
    Any month in which the player did not play is missing from this dataset,
    because the dataset is built starting from player activity, so any "empty
    month" simply doesn't exist in this dataset.
    """

    data = (
        df.with_columns(
            pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate(interval).alias("month"),
            first_month=pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate(interval).min().over("char"),
        )
        .unique(subset=["char", "month"])
        .with_columns(pl.lit(True).alias("has_played"))
    )
    return data



data = make_data(df)




Since we want to predict the behavior a player will have over a single month, our target variable will be grouped by “user-month” (e.g., ID153_2026-12). However, not all players will play at least once every month, so by relying exclusively on the historical data we would be missing samples; to get around this problem we generate a char_month dataset that contains all unique combinations of users and months by executing the cross-product between the unique users and the range of months.







NoneCross product (click to expand)





The cross product between two sets (in this case, months and unique users) builds a new set where each element in the first set is paired with all elements in the second set.

def make_user_month(df, interval="1mo"):
    """
    Create a DataFrame with all unique combinations of users and months.
    This will be used to ensure that we have a row for each user for each month
    in the range of the dataset, even if the user did not play in that month.

    This is done with a cross-product between the unique users and the range of months.

    This function is artificially generating months past the last month in the dataset.
    This is because we are also adding lagged features with lags of up to 3 months.
    At train time, we have access to all the information. If we try to predict churn
    for one of the months we have lagged information for, the model should not crash.
    It will still be missing the information "for the current month", but the
    lagged information will be available.
    This is more a sanity check than anything else.

    Note that since the months are generated from the range of the dataset, they
    may include months prior to a user's first activity. These will need to be
    filtered out later.
    """

    months = pl.datetime_range(
        start=df.select(pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate(interval).min())
        .collect()
        .item(),
        end=df.select(
            # Adding 3 months to the end of the range because we are adding
            # lagged features up to 3 months.
            pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate(interval).max().dt.offset_by("3mo")
        )
        .collect()
        .item(),
        interval=interval,
        closed="both",
        eager=True,
    )

    char_month = (
        df.with_columns(month=pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate(interval))
        .select("char")
        .unique()
        .join(months.to_frame(name="month").lazy(), how="cross")
    )
    return char_month

user_month.collect()

The grid extends three months past the end of the data. These extra months only exist so that lagged features can be computed on months without data, and the rows are dropped later because their target is unknown.
Now that we have all the combinations (character, month), we can join back the prepared data to mark all the months in which each character was found online, and marking all others with has_played=False.
Additionally, the resulting rows are filtered to remove all pairs (char, month) whose month precedes the character’s first month. We should not have a row about a character’s playtime in January if they started playing in August!
Then we add the churn information. After sorting by month, prev_played is the has_played flag of the previous month for the same character (False for the first month), churn marks the characters absent in both months, and churn_next is churn shifted one month back within each character. The last month in the data has no “next month” to look at, so its churn_next is left empty.






NoneAdd the churn columns (click to expand)







def add_churn(user_month, data):
    """
    Add churn information to the user-month DataFrame by merging it with the actual
    play data. The resulting DataFrame will have a "has_played" column indicating
    whether the user played in that month. Any missing values in "has_played" are
    filled with False: missing values mean that the player did not play in that
    particular month.

    It also adds the "churn" column (churned as of this month: absent this month
    and the previous one) and the "churn_next" column, the prediction target:
    the value of "churn" in the *following* month. Features for a given month are
    built from the previous month's data, so the target cannot be the churn
    status of the same month: that status includes "absent last month", which
    is exactly what the features reveal. "churn_next" is null for the last
    month in the data, because the following month has not been observed.
    """

    last_month = data.lazy().select(pl.col("month").max()).collect().item()

    df_with_user_month = (
        user_month.join(
            data,
            on=["char", "month"],
            how="left",
        )
        .with_columns(pl.col("has_played").fill_null(False))
        .with_columns(first_month=pl.col("first_month").min().over("char"))
        .filter(pl.col("first_month") <= pl.col("month"))
        .select(
            "char",
            "month",
            "has_played",
            "first_month",
        )
        .sort(["char", "month"])
        .with_columns(
            # has_played in the previous month for this character
            prev_played=pl.col("has_played").shift(1).over("char").fill_null(False)
        )
        .with_columns(
            # churn = absent this month AND absent last month
            # null on a character's first month is filled with False
            churn=pl.col("prev_played").is_not_null()
            & ~pl.col("has_played").fill_null(False)
            & ~pl.col("prev_played").fill_null(False)
        )
        .with_columns(
            churn_next=pl.when(pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("1mo") <= last_month)
            .then(pl.col("churn").shift(-1).over("char"))
            .otherwise(None)
        )
    )
    return df_with_user_month

r.collect()

Finally, we can put everything together in a single function that takes the historical data as input and returns a dataset with the churn indication as output. It also calls remove_unrealistic_entries, a safety check that removes the rows preceding a character’s first month and selects the final columns. Rows without a target are dropped, since they can be used neither for training nor for evaluation:


def build_churn_dataset(historical_data):
    # Load the dataset
    data = make_data(historical_data)
    # Add the combinations of user months
    user_month = make_user_month(historical_data)
    churn_data = add_churn(user_month, data)
    churn_data = remove_unrealistic_entries(churn_data, data)
    # Rows whose target is unknown (the last observed month and the padding
    # months after it) cannot be used to train or evaluate a model.
    return churn_data.filter(pl.col("churn_next").is_not_null()).collect()

title: Predicting player churn in an MMORPG (WoW)
section: 2 Setting up the ML pipeline
text:
2 Setting up the ML pipeline
Before starting with feature engineering and actually training the model, it’s worth spending some time understanding the scenario we are in.
The main factor that complicates this scenario is the fact that we are dealing with sequential data points, which are therefore not independent of each other: the position of a player at a time T is strongly correlated with their position at time T+1.

2.1 Building a custom splitter
For this reason, we need to use a splitter that returns sequential splits. A common example of this is scikit-learn’s TimeSeriesSplit. TimeSeriesSplit works by splitting the entire dataset in a given number of splits; during cross-validation, at step K the splitter returns the first k splits as the train split, and the k+1 split as the validation split.





Source
A downside of TimeSeriesSplit is that the splitter assumes uniformly distributed samples, so that each singular split has the same size as the others. This is a problem for our scenario: our samples are (character, month) pairs, and the number of characters in each month is never constant and indeed increases over time:





For this reason, we need to define a custom splitter that is aware of the constraints we are working with. Given that we are working month-by-month, each split should contain all the characters that played in a specific month, and should be able to do so regardless of the fact that the number of characters changes.
There is a second constraint: the target of a row is the churn status of the following month, so it is only known one month later. If the training set included the rows of the month right before the test month, their targets would be computed from the activity in the test month. The splitter therefore leaves a one-month gap between the last training month and the test month.
This is what we implement here:


The boundaries of the experiment are defined in main.py: split points go from 2006-02-01 to 2008-10-01, and each test month is the one following its split point. The last test month is the latest one whose target is fully observed.




class Splitter:
    """
    Iterates over the months. For each split point, the test month is the
    following month: it is the month during which we would score users and act
    on the ones marked as "churn risks".

    The target of a row (churn_next) is the churn status of the month after it,
    so it is only known one month later. The training set therefore stops one
    month before the split point: a row from the split point month would have a
    target computed from the test month.
    """

    def split(self, user_month, has_played=None, interval="1mo"):
        # the target is not needed in this splitter since we are only splitting
        # based on the month
        del has_played
        time_range = pl.date_range(MIN_DATE, MAX_DATE, interval, eager=True)
        for split_point in time_range:
            # I can either use dateutils.relative delta
            # test_month = split_point + relativedelta(months=1)
            # Or do this with polars which is more consistent with the rest of the code
            test_month = pl.Series([split_point]).dt.offset_by(interval).first()
            last_train_month = (
                pl.Series([split_point]).dt.offset_by("-" + interval).first()
            )
            # Train indices are up to last_train_month, included
            train_idx = (
                user_month.with_row_index("idx")
                .filter(pl.col("month") <= last_train_month)["idx"]
                .to_list()
            )
            # Test indices are for the month after split_point
            test_idx = (
                user_month.with_row_index("idx")
                .filter(pl.col("month") == test_month)["idx"]
                .to_list()
            )
            if train_idx and test_idx:
                print(f"Working on month {split_point}")
                yield train_idx, test_idx

    def get_n_splits(self, X, y):
        return sum(1 for _ in self.split(X, y))


Like all other scikit-learn splitters, our splitter is a generator that, given X and y (user_month and the target in our case), returns the indices of the samples that should be used in each split.

title: Predicting player churn in an MMORPG (WoW)
section: 3 Building the pipeline
text:
3 Building the pipeline

3.1 Generating the features
The features of a row at month M are computed from the activity of month M-1 only. They fall in a few groups:

fixed attributes of the character: race and class;
session features: skrub’s SessionEncoder groups consecutive heartbeats of a character into sessions, which gives the number of sessions in the month, and the total, average and standard deviation of their duration, and the average start and end time;
player features: highest level, number of distinct zones and guilds, most frequent zone, first and last guild;
playerbase features: average level and number of active players of the character’s class;
optionally, location features: how rare the zones visited by the character are, how much time is spent in “hub” zones that everyone visits, and how evenly the time is spread across zones (Gini coefficient);
lagged features: the value of every feature one or more months earlier, plus the month-to-month difference of numeric features, so that the model can see trends.

The functions that compute them live in adding_features.py. The function below loops over the months, and for each one filters the historical data down to the previous month before building the features. Because lagged features need each character’s complete timeline, the feature table is built once for every (character, month) pair, independently of the cross-validation split, and each split only selects its rows from it.






NoneFull feature engineering function (click to expand)







def filter_df_by_month(df, month):
    return df.filter(pl.col("month") == month)


def build_feature_table(
    historical_data,
    session_gap=30,
    use_location=True,
    add_gini=False,
    interval="1mo",
    lags=(1, 2),
):
    """
    Build the feature table for every (char, month) pair.

    This function makes sure that we are only ever using historical data up to
    the given month - 1 month. This is to avoid any leakage in the data.

    It builds the table for every (char, month) pair a character could appear
    in (not just the rows asked for by a given CV fold), because lagged
    features need each character's full monthly timeline: a CV fold's X may
    contain a single month (e.g. the test fold), which would otherwise leave
    every lag/diff column null.
    """
    features_by_month = []

    # Create a session encoder. The gap is a hyperparameter that can be tuned.
    # This encoder is used as a stateless transformer so it is refitted for every
    # month
    session_encoder = SessionEncoder(
        split_by="char", timestamp_col="timestamp", session_gap=session_gap * 60
    )
    historical_data = historical_data.with_columns(
        month=pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate(interval)
    ).lazy()

    # Every (char, month) pair a character could appear in, whether or not they
    # played that month: the full grid lag/diff features are built over.
    user_month = build_churn_dataset(historical_data).select("char", "month").lazy()
    # Adding fixed features: these features are fixed by character so they don't
    # change over time.
    user_month = user_month.join(
        historical_data.select("char", "race", "charclass").unique("char"),
        on="char",
        how="left",
        maintain_order="left",
    ).collect()

    # This is used to add the historical data up to the given month.
    # Sorting months is not needed, but forces a consistent order (better for debugging)
    for month in user_month["month"].unique().sort():
        this_month_X = filter_df_by_month(user_month, month)

        # Selecting only the entries in the historical data from the month before
        # the one I am building features for.
        # This means that if the row's month is April, then the historical data
        # is filtered to keep only the rows from March. Shifting the data forward
        # by one interval and filtering on the current month is equivalent to
        # saying "I want the rows for the current month - 1 month", but it's
        # easier to implement
        kept_historical_data = historical_data.with_columns(
            pl.col("month").dt.offset_by(interval)
        ).filter(pl.col("month") == month)

        # Session features: a session starts from a heartbeat, then it ends when
        # no more heartbeats are detected for session_gap minutes
        historical_data_sessions = session_encoder.fit_transform(
            kept_historical_data.collect()
        ).lazy()
        historical_data_sessions = get_session_duration(historical_data_sessions)

        # General features: add session based and playerbase features
        df_with_features = add_general_features(
            this_month_X.lazy(), historical_data_sessions
        )

        # Location features can be useful but take much longer to generate
        if use_location:
            # Grouping by character and zone so that I can get the time spent in each zone
            # Even if users leave the zone, this lets me find how much time a user spends in
            # a given zone
            session_encoder_zone = SessionEncoder(
                split_by=["char", "zone"],
                timestamp_col="timestamp",
                session_gap=session_gap * 60,
                suffix="session_id_zone",
            )
            # Zone-session features: a session lasts from the first time a character
            # enters a zone to the moment it leaves it
            # This is useful to get zone-specific features
            historical_data_zone_sessions = session_encoder_zone.fit_transform(
                kept_historical_data.collect()
            ).lazy()
            historical_data_zone_sessions = get_session_duration(
                historical_data_zone_sessions,
                session_column="timestamp_session_id_zone",
            )
            df_with_features = add_location_features(
                df_with_features,
                historical_data_zone_sessions,
                add_gini=add_gini,
            )
        else:
            df_with_features = df_with_features.collect()
        features_by_month.append(df_with_features)
        assert len(df_with_features) == len(this_month_X)

    feature_table = pl.concat(features_by_month, how="vertical")
    to_fill = pl.col("monthly_total_session_duration", "monthly_avg_session_duration")
    feature_table = feature_table.with_columns(
        to_fill.fill_null(pl.duration(seconds=0))
    )
    if lags is not None:
        feature_table = add_lagged_features(feature_table, lags=lags)
    return feature_table


def add_features(X, feature_table):
    """Attach this CV fold's (char, month) rows to the precomputed features."""
    return X.join(
        feature_table, on=["char", "month"], how="left", maintain_order="left"
    )







3.2 Putting everything together in a Data Op






TipLoading and downsampling the file (click to expand)





load parses the raw .txt heartbeat logs itself – parsing is a node of the plan, not a separate pre-processing script – then downsamples the result to reduce execution time. We need to be deliberate with how we sample the data: rather than choosing a random subset of the values in the dataset, we need to be careful to select a subset of characters and keep all the rows for those characters. This ensures that we have reliable information about all the characters.


def load(file_paths, fraction=0.1):
    """Parse the given raw ".txt" log files, then subsample by character."""
    df = parse_files(file_paths)
    if fraction == 1:
        return df.lazy()

    df = sample_by_user(df, fraction=fraction)
    return df.lazy()





The hyperparameters of the pipeline are declared with skrub’s choose_* functions: the session gap, whether to use location features, how many lags to add, and the learning rate of the model. They can then be tuned together with the rest of the plan.






TipFull Data Op construction script





def make_data_op(load_fraction=0.1, return_x=False):
    raw_files = skrub.var("raw_files")
    # Parsing the raw logs is a node of the plan like any other: the exact
    # same code path parses whichever files the "raw_files" environment
    # variable points to, whether that's the historical training set or a
    # held-out, never-before-seen set of files.
    historical_data = raw_files.skb.apply_func(load, fraction=load_fraction)
    # In the original data, "guild == -1" means "no guild", so I'm replacing -1
    # with nulls.
    historical_data = historical_data.with_columns(
        pl.when(pl.col("guild") == -1)
        .then(None)
        .otherwise(pl.col("guild"))
        .alias("guild")
    )

    user_month_has_played = historical_data.skb.apply_func(
        build_churn_dataset
    ).skb.set_name("query")
    X = user_month_has_played["char", "month"].skb.mark_as_X(cv=Splitter())
    y = user_month_has_played["churn_next"].skb.mark_as_y()

    # Hyperparameters
    session_gap = skrub.choose_from([30, 60, 15], name="session_gap")
    use_location = skrub.choose_bool(name="location_features")
    lags = skrub.choose_from(
        {"no": None, "1": (1,), "1_2": (1, 2), "1_2_3": (1, 2, 3)}, name="lags"
    )

    # Built from the full historical data (a plain, non-X node), independent of
    # the CV fold split of X, so lagged features always see each character's
    # complete monthly timeline regardless of which fold is being evaluated.
    feature_table = historical_data.collect().skb.apply_func(
        build_feature_table,
        session_gap=session_gap,
        use_location=use_location,
        add_gini=True,
        lags=lags,
    )
    all_features = X.skb.apply_func(add_features, feature_table)
    encoded = all_features.skb.apply(skrub.TableVectorizer())
    data_op = encoded.skb.apply(
        HGB(learning_rate=skrub.choose_float(0.1, 0.5, log=True)), y=y
    ).skb.with_scoring("roc_auc")
    # data_op = encoded.skb.apply(DummyClassifier(), y=y) #.skb.with_scoring("roc_auc")
    if return_x:
        return data_op, X
    return data_op






3.3 Running it
The data op is evaluated by passing a list of raw log file paths as input – parsing them is itself one of the plan’s nodes (see “Loading and downsampling the file” above). Here we cross-validate it on 10% of the characters of the historical (through October 2008) files:

data_op = make_data_op(load_fraction=0.1)
results = data_op.skb.cross_validate(environment=main.get_env("train"))

Note



The evaluation includes characters that were already absent in the previous month: predicting that they will remain absent is easy. A stricter evaluation would only score the characters that were still active, which are the ones that could actually be retained.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
section: The example in one slide
text:
The example in one slide

Dataset: WoWAH — ~11M timestamped “heartbeats” (one snapshot every ~10 min, 2006–2009, 91k avatars)
Task: predict whether a player churns (no activity) in month M+1
Unit of analysis: the (character, month) pair, built as a cross-product grid
Features: sessionization (SessionEncoder), monthly aggregates, zone-rarity / Gini location features, lag & diff features
Model: HistGradientBoostingClassifier + TableVectorizer, month-by-month temporal CV
Glue: everything assembled as a single skrub Data Op


The pipeline lives in main.py (with draft.qmd as the write-up version). It loads raw logs from a parquet file, builds churn labels with add_churn.py, engineers features in adding_features.py / location_features.py, and assembles the whole thing into a skrub DataOp via make_data_op(). Each of the following slides is a pain point a data scientist hits in this kind of project, and how the skrub DataOps design (per the user guide in skrub/_docs/) addresses it.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
section: Pain point 1 — Leakage in temporal feature engineering
text:
Pain point 1 — Leakage in temporal feature engineering

Features must only use data available at scoring time: history is filtered with a 2-month offset before the target month
Session detection and aggregations are stateful w.r.t. time: doing them once on the full table leaks the future
sklearn Pipeline cannot do this: X/y must exist before the pipeline starts, and wrangling lives outside
skrub docs warn explicitly: aggregation can introduce data leakage → wrap it in the DataOps plan
In the example: X and y are cut inside the plan (mark_as_X / mark_as_y), so each CV fold re-runs the feature code on training data only


This is the central difficulty of the example (main.py:90-186). If the target month is April, features may only be built from February data and earlier (main.py:136-143). The skrub sessionization doc (modules/multi_column_operations/sessionization.rst) carries a warning box saying aggregation leaks unless it is re-fit per fold — either wrapped in an sklearn transformer or done “with the skrub Data Ops framework”. DataOps bind the whole wrangling DAG to the prediction, so skb.cross_validate() re-executes the leakage-safe steps inside every fold automatically, instead of the user hand-rolling fold-by-fold feature construction.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
section: Pain point 2 — Cross-validation that respects irregular time
text:
Pain point 2 — Cross-validation that respects irregular time

Off-the-shelf TimeSeriesSplit assumes folds of equal size
Here the number of (char, month) rows grows every month — folds are unbalanced by nature
So the repo writes a custom splitter: expanding window over months, test = the following month only (main.py:46-74)
With DataOps: one line plugs it in — skb.mark_as_X(cv=Splitter())
The same splitter is then honored by cross_validate, train_test_split, randomized search, and scoring — no per-fold orchestration code


The custom Splitter (main.py:46) iterates month by month, yields train indices up to the split point and test indices for the next month. In a vanilla setup, the user would have to drive CV manually (loop over folds, build features per fold, fit, score). In the DataOps plan, mark_as_X(cv=Splitter()) (main.py:219) makes the splitter part of the estimator-like object, so skb.cross_validate() (main.py:259) and the Optuna search reuse it consistently. The docs (tuning_validating_data_ops.rst) also show how extra splitter arguments (e.g. groups) can be passed through mark_as_X.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
section: Pain point 3 — Tuning wrangling choices, not just model knobs
text:
Pain point 3 — Tuning wrangling choices, not just model knobs

Real choices live in the feature code: session_gap (15/30/60 min), include location features?, add Gini?, which lags?
These are not model hyperparameters — they are data pipeline decisions with big performance and runtime impact
DataOps: drop choices inline where the value is used — choose_from, choose_bool, choose_float(log=True)
One call turns the whole DAG into a search: skb.make_randomized_search(backend="optuna", ...) (main.py:267-280)
The repo shows the payoff: a persistent Optuna study (wowah_churn_study.db), results inspectable across runs


In make_data_op() (main.py:222-228), session_gap, use_location, add_gini and lags are declared with choose_from / choose_bool, and the model’s learning_rate with choose_float(0.1, 0.5, log=True). The hyperparameter tuning doc (validation/hyperparameter_tuning.rst) explains the principle: replace values with choice objects, and the same plan serves previews, defaults (describe_defaults), grid/randomized search, and Optuna. Crucially, choices placed inside wrangling functions get tuned too — impossible with a vanilla sklearn grid search over the final estimator.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
section: Pain point 4 — One pipeline object, many inputs, deployable
text:
Pain point 4 — One pipeline object, many inputs, deployable

Multi-input pipelines (raw log file path, churn table, config) are usually scattered across scripts with brittle glue
The example treats even the file path as an input: skrub.var("historical_data_file")
apply_func inserts arbitrary Python (loading, sampling, churn-label construction) as graph nodes
The final DataOp behaves like one sklearn estimator: .fit(), save, load, skb.eval(env), skb.cross_validate(env)
Production: replay the exact trained DAG on a new month — no re-implementation drift


make_data_op() (main.py:206) starts from a path variable, applies load (which subsamples by user), fixes the guild == -1 sentinel, builds churn labels, marks X/y, adds features, vectorizes, and fits HGB — one object. cross_validate() and evaluate() just pass different environments ({"historical_data_file": ...}) to the same plan (main.py:259-287). The docs’ what_are_data_ops.rst frames this as: a DataOp is a complete pipeline from data loading to prediction that can be fitted, tuned, cross-validated and saved like a scikit-learn estimator; data_ops_vs_alternatives.rst contrasts this with Pipeline, which is a linear sequence on a single table with a fixed row count.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
section: Pain point 5 — Debugging a complex DAG
text:
Pain point 5 — Debugging a complex DAG

With cross-products, two SessionEncoders, joins, lags… a join bug surfaces far from its cause
Eager previews: pass a value to var() and every node shows its result immediately — errors surface at the offending step
skb.full_report() emits an HTML report: every node’s name, description, predecessors, fitted estimator, and data preview
On failure, the report shows the offending node and the traceback
describe_steps, describe_param_grid, describe_defaults document the plan as it grows


The example’s pipeline has deep, branchy nodes (churn cross-product grid, session and zone-session encoders, rarity/Gini features, lag/diff expansion). The docs (basics/using_previews.rst, ml_pipeline/evaluating_debugging_data_ops.rst) describe exactly this workflow: previews catch errors early (e.g. a wrong column name in a Polars expression fails right away), and full_report() produces a browsable HTML execution report (stored under skrub_data/execution_reports by default). This replaces the usual print/pytest-debug loop on a multi-stage dataframe pipeline.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
section: Pain point 6 — Big data: subsampling and caching
text:
Pain point 6 — Big data: subsampling and caching

11M rows → interactive development must be fast, but sampling must preserve players’ full trajectories (sample_by_user, not random rows)
Feature building (build_feature_table) is very expensive — naive re-runs during search would explode cost
DataOps: skb.subsample() for development is automatically off for real eval / cross_validate runs
Caching (skrub.set_config(cache=True)) persists expensive node results on disk across trials — changing only learning_rate doesn’t recompute features
In-memory reuse is free: the feature_table node is computed once per parameter set and shared (main.py:229-239)


load() (main.py:196-202) samples whole characters to keep trajectories intact — exactly the kind of domain-specific subsampling the docs’ subsampling page (ml_pipeline/subsampling_data.rst) anticipates, with the caveat that subsampling is “local” to the variable it is applied to. The caching doc (ml_pipeline/caching.rst) is the counterpart for cost: results of skb.apply / skb.apply_func nodes are keyed and persisted, so hyperparameter trials that share early steps (all feature construction) skip recomputation; no_cache=True and cache pruning (target_cache_size) give control. Caveat from the docs: cache invalidation of changed helper code is best-effort — delete the cache when actively editing.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
section: Pain point 7 — Stay in your dataframe API inside the plan
text:
Pain point 7 — Stay in your dataframe API inside the plan

Frameworks usually force you to leave Polars once you enter “pipeline land”
DataOps are transparent: Polars methods are called directly on DataOps (historical_data.with_columns(...), .collect(), indexing, joins)
Python control flow (for month in ...) can’t run eagerly on a DataOp → put it in @deferred / apply_func functions
Each such function appears as one graph node — good for reports and caching granularity
The example leans on this everywhere: build_churn_dataset, build_feature_table, add_features


basics/direct_access_methods.rst documents the “transparent DataOp” design: any non-.skb attribute/method goes to the underlying object, so the example writes idiomatic Polars throughout (main.py:211-216). basics/control_flow.rst explains the eager-vs-deferred rule: for over a DataOp raises, so loops live inside @skrub.deferred functions or are attached via skb.apply_func — in the example the whole per-month feature loop is deferred into build_feature_table (main.py:90). One hygiene rule from the docs: transformations must return new values, not mutate in place — Polars’ expression style fits this naturally.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
section: The open tension (discussion)
text:
The open tension (discussion)

main.py precomputes feature_table once on the full history, then joins it onto each fold’s X
Why: lag/diff features need each character’s complete monthly timeline — a single-month fold would leave every lag null (main.py:82-89 comment)
But the write-up admits: “kinda defeats the point of using data ops but I think it simplifies the code” (draft.qmd:419)
Strict per-fold feature building is leakage-proof but slow; the static table is fast but frozen per hyperparameter set
DataOps makes this trade-off explicit and inspectable: the DAG documents exactly what is recomputed per fold vs. cached/shared


This is the design decision the example is really about. Two strategies coexist: (1) build features inside the graph from X (draft.qmd’s add_features loop) — perfectly leakage-safe, recomputed per fold; (2) precompute a feature_table node from the full historical data (main.py:229-239) so lagged features see all months, then left-join each fold’s rows. Option (2) relies on the argument that features are keyed by (char, month ≤ cutoff) so no future data can leak into the fold’s rows — but the plan no longer enforces it mechanically; the guarantee lives in build_feature_table’s code. A natural follow-up: move the per-month filtering inside the plan and use skrub caching to recover speed, so leakage safety is structural rather than conventional.

title: Pain points simplified by skrub DataOps
section: Takeaways
text:
Takeaways



Pain point
skrub DataOps answer




Temporal leakage
Wrangling lives inside the plan, re-run per fold


Irregular time CV
Custom splitter via mark_as_X(cv=...)


Tuning data choices
choose_* inline + Optuna-backed search


Many inputs, one artifact
var() + one estimator-like DataOp


Debugging
Previews + full_report() per node


Big data
subsample() + disk caching


API freedom
Transparent Polars access, @deferred for logic




Closing summary: the sessionization example is a good stress test because it combines every hard part of applied ML — temporal structure, custom validation, heavy feature engineering, big data, and tuning of pipeline-level decisions. The skrub DataOps docs position the framework precisely where sklearn Pipeline stops: DAG-shaped, multi-input, leakage-aware, tunable end-to-end, and inspectable. The remaining open question (per-fold vs. precomputed features) is itself made visible by the plan structure rather than hidden in scripts.

title: Skrub Data Ops: an application to player churn
section: The game
text:
The game



World of Warcraft (WoW) is MMORPG released in 2004 by Blizzard Entertainment.
Players create character avatars to navigate the open game world and perform various activities.
Players level up their characters to make them more powerful.
A single player may have multiple avatars.





World of Warcraft original cover

title: Skrub Data Ops: an application to player churn
section: The problem
text:
The problem

We are working with a subscription-based strategy where players pay a monthly fee to play the game.
Some players eventually stop playing, and thus stop paying their subscription.




We want to predict which players are likely to churn in the next month, in order to enact some measure to keep them from leaving.
A player churns if they have no activity for two full months.





Our “unit of analysis” is a (player character, month) pair.
Each pair tells us whether the given player character played on the given month.

title: Skrub Data Ops: an application to player churn
section: Caveats
text:
Caveats

While we are interested in players, we have information only about their avatars. A player may stop playing with an avatar, but keep paying the subscription.
As this is past data, we cannot actually evaluate the effectiveness of whatever measure we decide to implement, so we can only try to predict player behavior.

text:
Pain point 1 - Data ingestion is part of the pipeline

Data is not in a clean format:

Heartbeats are in text files scattered over hundreds of folders
Logs need to be resampled to have (character, month) granularity

The same transformations (and all other learned states) need to be replayed on new data.
Boilerplate code and pre-processing scripts are brittle and prone to errors.

title: Skrub Data Ops: an application to player churn
section: The dataset
text:
The dataset



Training samples are plain text, with custom formatting.
A custom parser must be used to convert the samples and extract the correct dtypes.

Pain point 4 — Debugging a complex DAG

Data Ops work lazily: they need to evaluate all nodes in the DAG to run
Eager previews: pass a value to var() and every node shows its result immediately

On failure, the report shows the offending node and the traceback

title: Skrub Data Ops: an application to player churn
section: What are we here for?
text:
What are we here for?

The dataset: World of Warcraft Avatar history Dataset 1

World of Warcraft is a subscription-based online videogame.
The dataset collects player activity over 2005-2009.




The problem: Some players eventually stop playing, and thus stop paying their subscription.

A player churns if they have no activity for two full months.
We want to predict which players are likely to churn in the next month, in order to enact some measure to keep them from leaving.





Our “unit of analysis” is a (player character, month) pair.
Each pair tells us whether the given player character played on the given month.


Source

World of Warcraft Avatar history

~35.6M timestamped “character is active” lines (heartbeats).
Time range: 2005-12-31 / 2009-01-10 in the Taiwanese server.
Two expansions are included in the range:

The Burning Crusade (April 2007)
Wrath of the Lich King (November 2008).

Pain point 1 - Data preparation is part of the pipeline


Building the pipeline
def make_data_op():
    raw_files = skrub.var("raw_files")
    historical_data = raw_files.skb.apply_func(load)

    user_month_has_played = historical_data.skb.apply_func(
        build_churn_dataset
    ).skb.set_name("query")
    
    X = user_month_has_played["char", "month"].skb.mark_as_X(...)
    y = user_month_has_played["churn_next"].skb.mark_as_y()

    feature_table = historical_data.skb.apply_func(build_feature_table)
    encoded = feature_table.skb.apply(skrub.TableVectorizer())
    data_op = encoded.skb.apply(HGBC(), y=y)
    return data_op


Exporting the learner
...
data_op, X = make_data_op()
learner = data_op.skb.make_learner()
learner.fit(get_env("train"))

unseen_env = get_env("unseen")
predictions = learner.predict(unseen_env)

section: Pain point 3 — Cross-validation with irregular time splits
text:
Pain point 3 — Cross-validation with irregular time splits



Data Ops natively support custom splitters for splitting data in the DAG.
Custom splitters can use custom dataframe logic to select the samples
Splitters plugged in skb.mark_as_X(cv=Splitter()) are honored by cross_validate, train_test_split, randomized search, and scoring


class Splitter:
    def split(self, X, y=None):
        ...
        for split_point in ...:
            test_month = pl.Series([split_point]).dt.offset_by("1mo").first()
            train_idx = (
                X.with_row_index("idx")
                .filter(pl.col("month") <= split_point)["idx"]
            )
            test_idx = (
                X.with_row_index("idx")
                .filter(pl.col("month") == test_month)["idx"]
            )

title: Skrub Data Ops: an application to player churn
section: Pain point 4 — Tuning wrangling choices, not just model knobs
text:
Pain point 4 — Tuning wrangling choices, not just model knobs

Model choices are not limited to model hyperparameters: session_gap (15/30/60 min), include location features?, which lags?
These are data pipeline decisions, with big performance and runtime impact
Pipeline decisions modify the pipeline itself, and regular hyperparameter tuning does not work

title: Skrub Data Ops: an application to player churn
section: Pain point 4 — Tuning wrangling choices, not just model knobs
text:
Pain point 4 — Tuning wrangling choices, not just model knobs

With DataOps choices can be dropped inline, where the value is used — choose_from, choose_bool, choose_float(log=True)
One call to skb.make_randomized_search(backend="optuna", ...) turns the whole DAG into a search


Replace any value with a choice:

 X = data.drop(columns="target", errors="ignore").skb.mark_as_X()
 y = data["target"].skb.mark_as_y()
 pred = X.skb.apply(StandardScaler()).skb.apply(
-    LogisticRegression(C=1.0),
+    LogisticRegression(C=skrub.choose_float(0.1, 10.0, log=True)),
     y=y)
Tune data pipeline decisions, not only hyperparameters

X_enc = X.skb.apply_func(build_features,
+  additional_features=skrub.choose_bool()
 )
 pred = X.skb.apply(LogisticRegression())
